title: Better and Saner Grading Tip: Start with the End
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that efficient grading depends on knowing the purpose of each assignment before touching it. He contrasts two recurring tasks in his world history course. Kelly Gallagher's Article of the Week aims at building knowledge and increasing reading and writing volume, so he gives fast, whole-class or small-group feedback. The College Board's Document-Based Question essay aims at seven discrete writing skills, so he grades each with a seven-point rubric at four to six minutes apiece. The principle is that the purpose of the assignment dictates how it is graded, which lets a teacher spend time where it builds skill and save it where it does not. The post is an assessment and feedback argument grounded in curriculum objectives.
points: Efficiency in grading is defined as accomplishing the assignment's purpose with minimal wasted time.
Article of the Week serves knowledge and volume, so its feedback is general and mostly whole-class.
DBQ essays serve seven specific argument-writing skills, so they warrant rubric-based, individual grading.
Naming priorities for each assignment type is what makes grading both better and saner.
quotes: Grading is not fun. I do not like grading. Therefore, my goal in grading is always this: do it as efficiently as possible.
But in order for me to understand whether I'm efficient or not, I have to know what the point of grading this particular assignment is.
When I give feedback on an AoW, it's at the whole-class or small-group level — hardly ever the individual level — because skill-building isn't the top priority.
Build specific writing skills pertinent to effective, evidence-based, historical arguments. Namely, seven specific skills:
In general, these take me four to six minutes to grade, as I'm completing a seven point rubric (see Figure 2) and writing comments as appropriate.
In short, the purpose of an assignment dictates our approach to grading it. This helps us grade more efficiently, which in turns makes us better and saner at our work.
